title: Loadbench failure-mode & observability playbook
summary: Hands-on playbook for diagnosing and triaging anomalies observed during throughput benchmarking runs. Focuses on observability signals, reproducible run metadata, focused loadgen patterns for isolating failure modes, and quick mitigation steps.
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc is a pragmatic playbook for engineers running throughput benchmarks who hit unexpected behavior: throughput collapse, tail-latency spikes, noisy variance between runs, or nondeterministic failures. It prioritizes fast triage using a small set of observability signals and targeted load patterns to isolate the root cause rather than exhaustive profiling every time.

Intended audience:
- Engs running or automating loadbench runs
- On-call SREs called during benchmark regressions
- Performance-focused reviewers for model onboarding

High-level flow (one-page checklist):
1) Capture contextual metadata (automate this).
2) Re-run a minimal deterministic check (5-minute micro-run) to confirm issue is reproducible.
3) Collect targeted signals (GPU counters, kernel traces, allocator stats).
4) Execute focused load patterns to differentiate CPU/IO/GPU/NET/kv-cache problems.
5) Narrow with a single-problem hypothesis, validate, and remediate.

What to capture at test start (minimum metadata):
- run_id: bench-<YYYYMMDD>-<model>-<runtime>-<seed> (e.g., bench-20251102-gpt-small-rn2-seed42)
- git_sha: runtime repo + model-variant commit
- container image + tag (full digest)
- instance type and PCI topology (ex: g4dn.xlarge, 1xA10G, PCIe x16)
- driver versions: nvidia-driver, cuDNN, CUDA, libcudart
- kernel build info and distro
- model details: architecture, quantization (bits), kv-cache enabled, max_seq_length
- loadgen config: arrival pattern, target concurrency, prompt distribution, seed for RNG
- observability snapshot start timestamp

Minimum reproducibility run (5 minutes):
- Purpose: quickly confirm whether the problem is stable enough to investigate.
- Pattern: steady Poisson arrivals at observed production occupancy (use same seq-length mix).
- Warmup: short warmup of 30s at 20% target QPS to prime caches.
- Metrics to assert: 50th/95th/99th latency within expected bounds, throughput within +/- 5% of baseline.

Signals to collect (prioritize):
1) Token-level and request-level latency histograms (per-route).
2) System GPU metrics sampled 1s: util%, mem%, encoder/decoder kernel time if available.
3) nvml counters: SM util, memory used, encoder/decoder pct, power, PCIe RX/TX.
4) OS-level: iostat -x 1, sar 1 5, vmstat 1 5, top -b -n 1 (full capture).
5) Network: tcptrace/sniffing for retransmits; netstat for socket states if drop suspected.
6) Runtime telemetry: active batch sizes distribution, queue length, retry/fallback events, batching timeouts.
7) GC/allocator stats (if runtime uses managed languages): heap, GC pause times.
8) Logs: runtime error log, kernel selection logs, model loading/unloading events.

Quick triage mappings (if you see X, try Y):
- Symptom: Throughput plateaus and GPU util low (<40%) while CPU is pegged -> Likely CPU-side bottleneck (batching, serialization, telemetry hooks).
  Action: record per-request CPU use (perf top), disable optional middleware (e.g., tracing) and re-run.

- Symptom: Throughput drops and NVML shows memory spikes followed by OOMs -> Memory churn/kv-cache eviction issue or memory leak.
  Action: run with a smaller batch size and disabled KV cache; collect pmap and runtime allocator traces.

- Symptom: High tail latency with high variance, GPU util high ~95% but throughput low -> Kernel-level stalls or PCIe saturation.
  Action: capture nvprof-like flame graphs or Nsight sampling, query PCIe RX/TX metrics. Try increasing batch parallelism or change kernel selection (FP16 vs INT8 path).

- Symptom: Intermittent microbursts cause spikes -> Batching window mismatch or loadgen arrival burstiness.
  Action: run controlled microburst pattern (see Load patterns below), measure queue depth and batching latency.

- Symptom: Throughput drops on long sequences only -> KV-cache eviction churn or decoding looping.
  Action: run fixed sequence-length experiments to confirm. Capture kv-cache hit/miss counters.

Focused load patterns (short, fast experiments to isolate class of failures):
1) Fixed-seq steady: Single sequence length (e.g., 64 tokens) Poisson arrivals at target occupancy. Tests whether seq-length mixing is problem.
2) Long-only: Single length at tail length (e.g., 1024) to stress KV-cache and memory.
3) Microburst train: 10 bursts of 2s at 3x target QPS separated by 5s idle. Useful to provoke queueing/backpressure.
4) Staircase ramp: Rapid ramp up in steps (10%, 30%, 60%, 100%, 120%) hold 30s each to reveal nonlinear saturation.
5) Single-concurrency probe: Run with a fixed concurrency (N clients with synchronous calls) to see per-worker bottlenecks.
6) Serial cold-starts: repeatedly start runtime and send single request to measure model load time and IO interference.

Sample loadgen snippet (pseudo-JSON to copy into bench harness):
{
  "name": "microburst-train",
  "pattern": "burst",
  "burst_qps": "x3_target",
  "burst_duration_s": 2,
  "interval_s": 5,
  "seed": 1337,
  "prompts": "mix-prod-sample.json"
}

Warmup guidance (practical):
- Use a two-stage warmup: quick prime (30s low QPS) then measured ramp (2 min) to target. The quick prime fills KV caches; the ramp brings kernel JITs and memory pools to steady state.
- For quantized models or kernels that JIT, include a synthetic warmup that triggers the long-path (e.g., long sequence) once to ensure paths compile.
- Record warmup acceptance criteria: after warmup, running 30s steady should show <3% throughput variance. If not, extend warmup.

Automated acceptance assertions (add these to CI):
- No >1% request error rate during run.
- 99th percentile latency < threshold for model+instance class.
- GPU util difference between two identical runs < 5%.
- Throughput drift compared to baseline < 7% (unless testing for scale).

Tooling & commands (cheat sheet):
- nvtop / nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o DT 1
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 1
- perf record -a -g -- sleep 60 && perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf.svg
- python runtime/telemetry/export_batch_dists.py --run-id=...
- iostat -xz 1 10 > iostat.log
- ss -s to check socket queues
- docker logs --timestamps --tail 200 <runtime-container>

When to escalate to a deep profile:
- If quick triage cannot reduce hypothesis space (GPU vs CPU vs IO) in three focused experiments.
- If problem reproducible across instance types or model variants.

Deep profile checklist (if escalated):
- Capture pprof traces from runtime on a 60–120s window.
- Capture GPU kernel timeline with Nsight Systems.
- Run microbench kernels on-device (small harness of GEMM/softmax ops) to validate driver/compiler behavior.
- Collect full OS perf counters (cache-misses, context switches).

Example incident timeline (realistic note-style):
- 2025-10-21 10:03: steady bench at 8000 TPS drops to 3500 TPS within 90s.
- Collected nvml: GPU util dropped from 92% to 34; PCIe TX spikes preceding drop.
- Hypothesis: unexpected PCIe DMA stalls when model kv-cache reaches threshold.
- Re-ran long-only test -> reproduced. Disabling kv-cache removed regression.
- Root cause: runtime observed a pathological eviction pattern in the LRU causing large backend memory copies. Patch landed to reduce eviction frequency (PR #678).

Common pitfalls and anti-patterns:
- Trusting a single long run instead of multiple short reproducible checks.
- Ignoring kernel/driver changes between runs. Always record driver versions.
- Increasing target concurrency to mask batching inefficiencies (you only hide the symptom).

Notes to engineer running first triage:
- When in doubt, make the experiment simpler: fewer clients, single sequence length, deterministic seed. Complexity hides the signal.
- Keep a run notebook (append to the run_id) with every hypothesis and result; these are cheap to keep and invaluable later.

Appendix A: example run-id convention and minimal metadata file (bench-metadata.json as a single-line example):
{
  "run_id": "bench-20251102-gpt-medium-rn2-seed42",
  "git_sha": "a1b2c3d4",
  "image": "registry.redwood/v1/runtime@sha256:deadbeef",
  "instance": "a100-40g-x2",
  "driver": "nvidia-driver-525.85",
  "loadgen": "microburst-train-v3",
  "notes": "triggered after nightly regression"
}

Appendix B: quick checklist for CI integration (short):
- Auto-generate run_id and collect metadata on every run.
- Store metrics + nvml snapshot as run artifacts.
- Run minimal reproducibility suite on failure before alerting humans.
- Attach run artifacts and a short hypothesis to the alert.

Open questions / TODOs (future work):
- Add GPU kernel classification to runtime logs (label major kernels: attention, MLP, softmax).
- Integrate hardware perf counters into our centralized traces for easier correlation.
- Implement an automated microburst regression detector (alg that runs over QPS time series).

If you're using this doc: append your triage notes below this file (brief bullets) so we can build a small corpus of real incidents and fixes that help refine heuristics.

End of playbook.
